_comment: Ready-made skills. Each fits every project ('any') or one pack. Setup enables every skill that fits the installed packs, unless the user declines it: the 'Library skills' line of the Setup interview in docs/DECISIONS.md names it after 'left out' with the reason (the setup gate checks this). 'ask' is the question that confirms the fit; 'default' is the recommendation. Every folder in library/skills needs an entry here (audit). 'requirements' are the checks that prove the skill was followed; enable adds them to tools/hooks/requirements.json.

skills.name: orchestrate
skills.good: Big jobs split across several AI helpers or many sessions, like researching many topics at once.
skills.costs: Extra bookkeeping (a ledger file) that a small, one-step project never needs.
skills.does: When a big job is split across several AI helpers, it keeps a list of who does what and checks each part before calling it done.
skills.outcome: Long jobs finish completely instead of stalling halfway, and you can see where each part stands.
skills.summary: Coordinates long multi-step or multi-agent runs with a ledger, check-ins, re-briefs, shared-resource queues and a verify-before-accept gate.
skills.ask: Will this project often run long jobs split across several agents or sessions that need tracking until they are all verified?

requirements.message: Orchestrate skill: run node skills/orchestrate/scripts/ledger.mjs check <ledger> and act on everything it lists before reporting.

skills.name: backend-patterns
skills.good: The project has, or will have, its own server, API or database.
skills.costs: Nothing for projects without server code; it only adds reading time when unused.
skills.does: Follows proven patterns when writing server code: APIs, databases, errors, logins and logging.
skills.outcome: Server code that is more consistent, safer and easier to change later.
skills.summary: Stack-neutral patterns for server code: layers, API design, queries, errors, caching, background jobs, access checks and logging, with a Done-when checklist.
skills.ask: Will this project have its own server, API or database code?

requirements.message: Backend-patterns skill: server code changed without tests. Add tests for the service logic and one success and one failure per endpoint, and run them.

skills.name: codebase-map
skills.good: The code is large, unfamiliar, or will grow past what one session can keep in mind.
skills.costs: The map must be refreshed after big changes, or it goes stale. Little gain for a handful of files.
skills.does: Reads an unfamiliar or large codebase once and writes a map: where things start, how parts connect, where to change what.
skills.outcome: Faster, safer changes in code you or the AI did not write.
skills.summary: Maps an unfamiliar or large codebase (entry points, module dependencies, main flows, git hot spots, where to change what) and saves it to docs/ for later sessions.
skills.ask: Is this an existing or large codebase that you or the agent will need to find your way around?

requirements.message: Codebase-map skill: save the map to docs/codebase-map.md (with date, commit, tools used and unknowns) so later sessions reuse it.

skills.name: frontend-design
skills.good: The project has screens, pages or reports people look at: one place for design, wording, accessibility and handoff, all following the same rules.
skills.costs: A short design plan before building adds a few minutes per screen. An accessibility review without a real screen-reader test is not a full guarantee.
skills.plain: Design help for screens and pages
skills.does: Designs new screens on purpose, and also critiques existing designs, keeps colors and components consistent, writes button and error text, checks accessibility, and writes specs for developers.
skills.outcome: Screens look distinctive and polished, work for keyboard and screen-reader users, use the same words and styles everywhere, and can be built without guessing.
skills.summary: One design skill split by situation: A designs a new screen, B critiques a design, C keeps a design system consistent, D writes interface text, E reviews accessibility against WCAG 2.2 AA, F writes a developer handoff spec.
skills.ask: Will this project have screens or pages people look at, and do you want help designing them, reviewing them, wording them, checking they are accessible, or handing them to a developer?

requirements.message: Frontend-design skill: name the section used ("Frontend design: <letter>"). For section A, also write the design plan (direction, color, type, layout, first view, motion, the one memorable thing), say in the answer what it is, then run the gui-review-loop.

skills.name: mcp-builder
skills.good: You want AI assistants to use your app's data or actions directly.
skills.costs: Building and securing a server is real work; skip it unless you need AI tools to plug into the app.
skills.plain: Connect AI tools to your app
skills.does: Builds an MCP server: a standard plug that lets AI assistants use your app's data and actions.
skills.outcome: AI assistants can work with your app directly.
skills.summary: Designs, builds, tests and documents a Model Context Protocol server in any language, with well-described tools, safe defaults and testing through real agent tasks.
skills.ask: Will this project build a server that lets AI agents use its data or actions (an MCP server)?

requirements.message: Mcp-builder skill: save the server's tools/list result and run node skills/mcp-builder/scripts/lint-tools.mjs on it until it reports no problems.

skills.name: repo-setup
skills.good: You often download or clone code that has to be installed and run.
skills.costs: Not needed when the project starts from scratch and has its start command written down.
skills.does: Installs, builds and runs code you downloaded, and writes down the one command that starts it.
skills.outcome: Cloned projects run on your machine without trial and error.
skills.summary: Gets a cloned or unfamiliar repo to install, build, run and pass its tests locally on any stack, and records it as one start command.
skills.ask: Will this project start from existing code that has to be installed and run on this machine?

requirements.message: Repo-setup skill: record in docs/STATUS.md what was set up, the baseline test results, what is missing and what is next.

skills.name: security-hardening
skills.good: The app stores other people's data, logins or payments, or will be public.
skills.costs: A multi-step project of its own; overkill for a personal tool that stays on one computer.
skills.does: Finds and fixes security weaknesses in an existing app, most dangerous first, with a test for each fix.
skills.outcome: An app that is much harder to break into or leak data from.
skills.summary: Runs a staged, risk-ranked hardening project on an existing app, with a regression test per fix and a re-review at the end.
skills.ask: Will this app handle other people's data, accounts or secrets, or be exposed to the internet?

requirements.message: Security-hardening skill: save the plan (threat model, inventory, ranked fixes) in docs/plans/ before fixing.

skills.name: commit-archaeologist
skills.good: The project keeps growing and older code gets changed: it explains why code exists before it is changed, so old fixes are not undone. Pays off once there are a few weeks of history.
skills.costs: None until used. Needs git history to read.
skills.does: Reads the history of a file to explain why a piece of code exists and what could break if it changes.
skills.outcome: Fewer accidents when changing old or unfamiliar code.
skills.summary: Explains why a file, function or block of code exists from the local git history (origin, timeline, reverts, companion files, intent words) in a short report with a confidence label and the risks of changing it.
skills.ask: Will you work in existing code with a git history, where it helps to know why something was written before changing or removing it?

requirements.message: Commit-archaeologist skill: open the report with the bottom line and a label, Confidence: high, medium or low, and back the origin, timeline and intent with commit hashes.

Commit-archaeologist skill: back the origin, the timeline and the intent with the commit hashes they come from (short hashes are fine). If the code has no history yet, say so and write "N/A(history-hashes): no commits touch it".

skills.name: compress-for-ai
skills.good: The AI's rules and guides grow long, or you use helper agents and want their notes and reports kept short.
skills.costs: Shortened files are harder for people to read, and each compression job takes a few extra steps (backup, check, fixes). Independent tests found modest savings on answers: about 8.5% fewer output tokens.
skills.plain: Shorter text for the AI, nothing lost
skills.does: Shortens the AI's own rules, guides and notes between AI helpers so they cost less to read. If you ask, it also gives you shorter answers. A check proves that no file path, name, number or "not" was changed.
skills.outcome: Cheaper, faster sessions. Text meant for you stays plain unless you ask for terse answers.
skills.summary: Shortens AI-facing text in three modes (AI-facing files, notes between agents, and terse replies only when the user opts in) at three levels (light, full, ultra). A zero-dependency protect check fails if any path, file name, URL, command, flag, code, identifier, number, date, version, quote, name marker, check tag, heading, frontmatter, table, list numbering or negation changed. Files get a verified backup in .cache/.
skills.ask: Do you want the agent to keep its own rules, guides and helper notes short and cheap to read, with a check that no file path, name, number or "not" ever changes, and terse answers for you only when you ask?

requirements.message: Compress-for-ai skill: run the protect check on every compressed file (compress-guard.mjs check <backup folder>, or protect-check.mjs <before> <after> for agent notes), fix every CHANGED line or restore the file, before reporting.

skills.name: teach
skills.good: You want to learn or understand things, not only get answers.
skills.costs: Answers take longer, because it checks understanding step by step.
skills.does: When you ask to learn something, it teaches one step at a time and checks you understand, instead of just giving the answer.
skills.outcome: You actually learn it, with quizzes or flashcards when you want them.
skills.summary: Helps the user really learn something instead of handing over answers, using proven methods (practice recall, worked examples, a hint ladder, feedback on their own attempts), makes quizzes, flashcards and study guides, keeps facts accurate, and respects graded work.
skills.ask: Do you want the agent to teach you step by step (checking you understand, with quizzes or flashcards on request) when you ask to learn or understand something?

requirements.message: Teach skill: end each reply with one question that asks the user to take the next step, or close the session with a "Learned:" line saying what they can now do.

skills.name: architecture
skills.good: Apps that will grow: choosing a database or framework, adding a service or a large feature, or code that keeps getting harder to change.
skills.costs: Writing a decision or design takes time that a tiny or throwaway app doesn't need.
skills.does: Helps make and write down big technical choices, design a new system before it is built, and list the code clean-ups worth doing in order.
skills.outcome: Choices are written down with their reasons, so they are not re-argued, and clean-up happens in small steps instead of a risky rewrite.
skills.summary: Three parts: record a decision with real options and a concrete reopen-if in docs/DECISIONS.md, design a system from load numbers to contracts and failure handling, and rank tech debt from evidence into docs/tech-debt.md with a plan paid alongside features.
skills.ask: Will this app face big technical choices, such as which database, framework or services to use, or grow large enough to need planned clean-ups?

requirements.message: Architecture skill: name the file written: the docs/DECISIONS.md row (part A), the design file in docs/specs (part B), or docs/tech-debt.md (part C).

skills.name: incident-response
skills.good: Apps or services that real users depend on while they are live.
skills.costs: Nothing until something breaks. A post-mortem takes an hour or so after a serious outage.
skills.does: When the live app breaks for its users, it stops the harm first, keeps a timeline, drafts updates for people, fixes the cause, and writes a blameless report afterwards.
skills.outcome: Outages end sooner, users hear what is going on, and the same problem doesn't come back because every lesson becomes a check.
skills.summary: Triage with a severity scale, limit the harm (rollback, flag, block) with the user's OK, drafted status updates, root-cause fix through debug/bugfix/release, and a blameless post-mortem in docs/incidents with typed actions that become checks.
skills.ask: Will people rely on this app or service while it is live, so that an outage would hurt them?

requirements.message: Incident-response skill: keep the incident file in docs/incidents/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>.md (level, timeline, impact, post-mortem) and name it in the answer.
Incident-response skill: say where the cause stands in a "Root cause: <what and why>" line, or "Root cause: not found yet" while the harm is still being stopped.

skills.name: data-analysis
skills.good: You will hand the AI spreadsheets, CSV or JSON files, survey results or other tables, and ask what they show.
skills.costs: Each data question takes a few extra steps (a profile, quality checks, a re-run before sharing). It does nothing for projects without data files.
skills.does: Looks over a data file first, checks it for problems, works out answers with real calculations, and makes honest charts, so every number can be traced back to the data.
skills.outcome: Answers, tables and charts from your data that you can trust and check, with the method stated next to each result.
skills.summary: Profiles new datasets (zero-dependency profile.mjs), checks quality, answers with computed statistics and stated uncertainty, queries with optional DuckDB or SQLite, builds honest static charts and dashboards, and re-runs and traces every number before sharing.
skills.ask: Will you ask the agent to analyse data files such as spreadsheets, CSV or JSON exports and report numbers or charts from them?

requirements.message: Data-analysis skill: compute every number with code run this turn (profile.mjs, a script, or a query), and say how in a 'How it was computed:' line naming the script or query and the row count. Numbers with no output behind them are removed or marked not verified.

skills.name: legal-review
skills.good: You regularly handle contracts, NDAs, vendor agreements, privacy requests or compliance questions and want a careful first pass before a lawyer or signer sees them.
skills.costs: It is not legal advice and can be wrong about the law; anything that matters still needs a qualified lawyer, and law lookups take extra research time.
skills.does: Reviews contracts and NDAs, checks plans against privacy and other rules, rates legal risk, drafts replies to legal requests and checks documents before signing, always saying when a lawyer is needed.
skills.outcome: You get an organized first read of legal documents, with suggested wording to change and a clear flag whenever something needs a real lawyer.
skills.summary: One skill for legal paperwork by situation: contract review against the user's own positions, NDA screening, compliance and privacy checks, risk rating, legal replies, vendor agreement status, briefs and meeting prep, and a signing checklist. Every result says it is not legal advice, lists when a lawyer is needed, and checks laws through the research skill.
skills.ask: Do you want the agent to help with contracts, NDAs, compliance questions and other legal paperwork (a first read only, never legal advice, and it tells you when you need a lawyer)?

requirements.message: Legal-review skill: say plainly that this is not legal advice, and list anything that needs a lawyer.

skills.name: marketing
skills.good: The project produces marketing material, campaigns, newsletters or web pages, or needs to track competitors and results.
skills.costs: Sourcing every claim and competitor fact makes answers slower, and without your own data it sets no targets and leaves placeholders instead of numbers.
skills.does: Checks and drafts marketing content in your brand voice, plans campaigns and email sequences, writes sourced competitor briefs, turns results into reports and audits a site's SEO.
skills.outcome: Marketing drafts and plans sound like your brand, and every number or competitor claim in them has a source or a clear placeholder.
skills.summary: One skill for marketing by situation: brand voice review with claim checks, campaign plans, drafts for any channel including email sequences, competitor briefs through the research skill, performance reports, and SEO audits. No invented statistics or benchmarks; publishing and sending need the user's OK.
skills.ask: Do you want the agent to help with marketing (brand voice checks, campaign plans, content and email drafts, competitor briefs, performance reports and SEO audits), with every claim sourced?

requirements.message: Marketing skill: name the brand voice used, and give every statistic, result, benchmark and competitor fact its source, or leave a visible placeholder ([stat needed: <what>, source?]).

skills.name: user-research
skills.good: You will plan interviews, surveys or usability tests, or turn notes, survey results, support tickets or reviews into findings.
skills.costs: Planning a study and counting every theme take longer than skimming notes. It adds nothing to projects that never learn from people.
skills.does: Plans interviews, surveys and usability tests that can answer a real question, and turns what people said into findings with counts and exact quotes.
skills.outcome: Findings you can trust: every theme counted, every quote traced to the notes, and people's names and contact details kept out.
skills.summary: Plans studies with people (the decision, the questions, the method and who takes part), runs them without leading questions, and synthesizes notes, survey exports and feedback into themes with "n of N" counts, exact quotes by participant ID, observations kept apart from interpretations, and stated limits. Uses the research skill's accuracy check.
skills.ask: Will you plan interviews, surveys or usability tests, or ask the agent to turn notes, survey results or feedback into findings?

requirements.message: User-research skill: give every theme its count as "n of N" with quotes traced to participant IDs, or, for a study plan, name the decision it informs.
